scenes.heading: Replication
scenes.narration: Replication keeps multiple copies of data across nodes so the system survives failures, serves reads locally, and stays available when a node goes down.

scenes.heading: Why we replicate
bullets: Durability: survive disk and node failures
Availability: promote a replica if the primary fails
Read scaling: spread reads across copies
Locality: serve users from a nearby region
scenes.narration: Replication provides durability by keeping data alive even when a disk or whole node fails. It provides availability because a replica can be promoted when the primary goes down. It scales reads by spreading query traffic across many copies. And it improves locality by placing copies near users so reads are served from a nearby region.

scenes.heading: Synchronous vs asynchronous

right.label: Asynchronous
points: Fast writes, may lose recent data

scenes.narration: With synchronous replication the primary waits for at least one replica to acknowledge before confirming a write, so a failover loses no committed data, but every write pays the round-trip latency cost. With asynchronous replication the primary acknowledges immediately and ships changes in the background, which makes writes fast but risks losing the most recent writes if the primary dies before they propagate. Many systems compromise with semi-synchronous replication to bound the data-loss window.

scenes.heading: Leader-based replication
scenes.narration: In leader-based replication all writes go to a single leader, which appends them to a replication log. That log is streamed to the follower replicas, which apply the same changes in order to stay in sync. Reads can be served by leader or followers depending on the consistency needed. If the leader fails, an election or controller promotes an up-to-date follower to become the new leader.

scenes.heading: Single-leader vs multi-leader
scenes.narration: Single-leader replication routes all writes through one node, which keeps the conflict story simple and gives one clear source of truth, but that leader can become a write bottleneck and a single point of failure until failover completes. Multi-leader replication lets multiple nodes, often one per region, accept writes, which improves write availability and locality, but it introduces the hard problem of resolving conflicting concurrent writes to the same key. Choose single-leader for simplicity and multi-leader only when multi-region write availability truly demands it.

scenes.heading: The replication lag problem
bullets: Async followers trail the leader briefly
A read from a lagging replica looks stale
Route recent reads to the leader to fix it
scenes.narration: Asynchronous replication means followers trail the leader by some amount of lag. If a client writes to the leader and then immediately reads from a lagging follower, its own update may appear to be missing, which is jarring and can look like a bug. This specifically breaks the read-your-writes guarantee. A common fix is to route reads that follow a recent write from the same user to the leader, or to a replica known to be caught up, so users always see their own changes.

scenes.text: Match replication mode to your recovery goals: synchronous for zero data loss, asynchronous for speed, quorums for balance.
scenes.narration: Match the replication mode to your recovery objectives, choosing synchronous when zero data loss matters, asynchronous when write speed matters, and quorum reads and writes when you need a tunable balance of both.
